items.prompt:
Read this story below.

My name is Sam. I live next door to a girl named Zoe. Yesterday, Zoe knocked on my door. 'Want to go ride bikes?' she asked. 'Sure!' I said. We rode to the park and back.

Who is the narrator? Is this first-person or third-person? Who else speaks?
items.answer: The narrator is Sam. This is first-person (uses 'I' and 'My'). Zoe also speaks: 'Want to go ride bikes?' Sam speaks in dialogue too: 'Sure!'

steps: Sam names himself in the first sentence: 'My name is Sam.' He uses 'I' throughout. First-person. Zoe speaks inside quotation marks. Sam also speaks inside quotation marks. The narration is Sam's voice; the dialogue is where the characters talk.

items.prompt:
Read this story below.

Marco kicked the ball into the goal. He cheered and punched the air. 'Yes!' he shouted.

Is the narrator first-person or third-person? What clue words tell you?
items.answer: Third-person. Clue words: 'Marco,' 'He,' 'he.' The narrator uses Marco's name and refers to him as 'he,' not 'I.'

steps: 'Marco' is a name, not 'I.' 'He' refers to Marco. Both show the narrator is outside the story. Third-person narrators use names and pronouns like he/she/they.

items.prompt:
Read this story below.

I had never been on a plane before. When the plane took off, my stomach flipped. I gripped the armrest hard. 'First time flying?' asked the man next to me. I nodded and smiled.

Who is the narrator? Is there another character who speaks? Who says more in this story, the narrator or the other character?
items.answer: The narrator is the unnamed 'I.' First-person. The man next to them says: 'First time flying?' The narrator says more overall because they narrate the whole story. The man has only one line.

steps: 'I had never,' 'my stomach,' 'I gripped,' 'I nodded' are all first-person narration. The man speaks once in quotation marks. The narrator tells the whole story and also nods in response. The narrator has more 'words' in the story.

items.prompt:
Read this story below.

Aisha opened her lunch box. Ben leaned over. 'What did you get?' he asked. 'Leftover pasta,' Aisha said. 'Lucky,' said Ben.

List every character who speaks and write what they say.
items.answer: Ben says: 'What did you get?' and 'Lucky.' Aisha says: 'Leftover pasta.'

steps: Ben speaks twice: 'What did you get?' and 'Lucky.' Aisha speaks once: 'Leftover pasta.' Their speech is inside quotation marks. The narrator (third-person) connects the dialogue with 'he asked,' 'Aisha said,' and 'said Ben.'

items.prompt:
Read this story below.

Maya looked at the sky. Dark clouds were coming. 'We should go in,' said Leo. 'Not yet,' Maya said. 'Just five more minutes.' Then the rain started.

Is the narrator first-person or third-person? How does the narrator differ from the characters who speak?
items.answer: The narrator is third-person (uses 'Maya,' 'Leo,' 'the sky'). The narrator describes the scene from outside. The characters (Leo and Maya) speak inside quotation marks, using 'I' and 'we' to refer to themselves.

steps: Narrator words: 'Maya looked,' 'Dark clouds were coming,' 'Then the rain started.' These are third-person observations. Characters speaking: Leo uses 'we' and Maya says 'Not yet' and 'Just five more minutes.' The narrator describes the scene; the characters speak directly to each other.

items.prompt:
Read this story below.

I am a cloud. I drift across the sky every day. Sometimes I am white and soft. Other times I turn gray and heavy with rain. 'Move along,' the wind says to me. 'I will when I am ready,' I say back.

Who is the narrator? What is unusual about this narrator?
items.answer: The narrator is a cloud, speaking in first-person (uses 'I'). What is unusual is that a cloud cannot really think or speak. The author chose an object as the narrator to tell the story from the cloud's point of view.

steps: 'I am a cloud' tells us directly. The cloud uses 'I' throughout. Clouds are not living things that can narrate stories. This is a creative storytelling choice where an object gets to speak. The wind also speaks in the story: 'Move along.'

items.prompt:
Read this story below.

Leo wanted to keep the baby bird he found. 'We cannot keep it,' his mom said. 'Why?' he asked. 'It belongs in the wild,' she said. Leo looked at the bird for a long time. He let it go.

How many characters speak? Is the narrator first-person or third-person?
items.answer: Three characters speak: Leo's mom says 'We cannot keep it' and 'It belongs in the wild.' Leo says 'Why?' The narrator is third-person, using 'Leo,' 'he,' 'his mom,' and 'she.'

steps: Mom speaks twice. Leo speaks once ('Why?'). Three total speech turns (two from mom, one from Leo). The narration outside the quotes uses names and pronouns like 'he' and 'she.' Third-person narration.

items.prompt:
Read this story below.

I walked into the old library. The smell of books was everywhere. A woman at the desk looked up. 'Can I help you?' she asked. 'Yes,' I said. 'I am looking for a book about stars.'

Write two sentences: one describing what the narrator says or does, and one describing what the other character says.
items.answer: What the narrator does: The narrator walks into the library and asks for a book about stars. What the librarian says: The librarian asks 'Can I help you?'

steps: Narrator actions: enters library, smells books, speaks to the librarian. Narrator's words in quotes: 'Yes' and 'I am looking for a book about stars.' Librarian's words in quotes: 'Can I help you?' The narrator is first-person.

items.prompt:
Read this story below.

Ben and Sam were best friends. They did everything together.

Then read this version:

I have a best friend named Sam. We do everything together.

How is the narrator different in each version?
items.answer: In the first version, the narrator is third-person (uses 'Ben' and 'They,' observing from outside). In the second version, the narrator is first-person (uses 'I' and 'We,' telling their own story from the inside). The same event feels different depending on who is telling it.

steps: Version 1: 'Ben and Sam' are named characters, viewed from the outside. 'They' is a third-person pronoun. Version 2: 'I' tells the story from inside. 'We' means the narrator and Sam together. The same friendship is described, but one is an outside view and one is an inside view.

items.prompt:
Read this story below.

Zoe's dog ran away. She searched the whole neighborhood, calling his name. Her neighbor Mr. Hill came outside. 'Are you looking for a brown dog?' he asked. 'Yes!' Zoe said. 'He is in my yard,' Mr. Hill said. Zoe ran to get him.

Is the narrator first-person or third-person? Name every character who speaks and write what they say.
items.answer: The narrator is third-person (uses 'Zoe,' 'She,' 'Her,' 'he'). Characters who speak: Mr. Hill says 'Are you looking for a brown dog?' and 'He is in my yard.' Zoe says 'Yes!'

steps: Narrator uses 'Zoe,' 'She,' 'Her' throughout. Third-person. Mr. Hill speaks twice. Zoe speaks once. All speech is in quotation marks. 'He asked' and 'said' are dialogue tags.

items.prompt:
Read this story below.

I love winter more than summer.

Now read this version:

Aisha loves winter more than summer.

If you could only read one of these sentences, which would you know more about: the narrator's feelings or Aisha's feelings? Explain.
items.answer: In the first sentence, you know the narrator's own feelings directly, because they use 'I.' In the second sentence, you know Aisha's feelings, but from the outside. Both tell you about feelings, but the first is more personal and direct because it comes from the person who feels it.

steps: First-person narration ('I love') gives direct access to the narrator's inner feelings. Third-person ('Aisha loves') tells us a fact about someone else, but it feels less immediate. Both convey the same information, but first-person feels more personal and immediate.

items.prompt:
Read this story below.

Marco was nervous. He took a deep breath. 'You can do this,' he told himself.

Is the narrator first-person or third-person? Who is speaking in the quotation marks?
items.answer: The narrator is third-person (uses 'Marco,' 'He,' 'himself'). The character speaking in the quotation marks is Marco, talking to himself. Marco is both the subject of the story and the one speaking.

steps: 'Marco was nervous' and 'He took' show third-person narration. The quote 'You can do this' is Marco's self-talk. 'He told himself' confirms it is Marco speaking to himself. It is unusual because the character speaks and the listener is also himself.

items.prompt:
Read this story below.

I remember the day I got my first bicycle. My dad ran alongside me. 'Keep pedaling!' he shouted. 'I am!' I yelled back.

How many people speak in this story? Name them and write what each says.
items.answer: Two people speak: the narrator says 'I am!' and the narrator's dad says 'Keep pedaling!' The narrator is first-person.

steps: Dad speaks: 'Keep pedaling!' Narrator speaks in dialogue: 'I am!' Two speakers. The narration is first-person ('I remember,' 'My dad,' 'I yelled').

items.prompt:
Read this story below.

Aisha was the narrator of the class play. 'Long ago,' she said, 'there was a little girl named Rose who lived near a big forest.'

Is the narrator of the story Aisha, or is the narrator of the play inside the quote someone else?
items.answer: The narrator of the story (the text we are reading) is third-person and tells us about Aisha. Aisha is telling a separate story inside the quotation marks, where she plays the narrator of the class play. There are two levels of narration.

steps: The text we are reading is narrated in third-person: 'Aisha was the narrator.' Inside Aisha's speech, she begins a different story: 'Long ago, there was a little girl.' That inner story has its own narrator (Aisha acting as narrator). There is a narrator telling us about Aisha, and Aisha telling us about Rose.

items.prompt:
Read this story below.

I was building a sandcastle when a wave knocked it down. I wanted to cry. Then a little boy walked over. 'Let me help,' he said. We built it back together, bigger than before.

Who is the narrator? Is the narrator first-person or third-person? Who else speaks?
items.answer: The narrator is an unnamed 'I.' First-person. A little boy also speaks: 'Let me help.' The narrator never names themselves, but tells their own story throughout.

steps: 'I was building,' 'I wanted to cry,' 'We built' are all first-person. The narrator does not name themselves. The little boy speaks once: 'Let me help.' Two voices: the first-person narrator and the little boy.
